analysis.one_liner: Bans phthalate plastic chemicals from food packaging and food-processing equipment.
analysis.headline: The bill banning phthalates from food packaging and processing equipment died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would ban ortho-phthalate chemicals — plastic softeners used in food tubing, packaging, gloves, and lid gaskets — from anything that touches food, two years after enactment, on the grounds that they leach into food and can harm fetal development. It would also require the FDA to review its other regulated products for phthalate exposure and publish the findings, with special attention to higher exposure among communities of color and workers. The bill never moved past its first committee stop.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant women, infants, and children would gain the most, since the bill's findings cite evidence that phthalates leaching from food equipment and packaging can harm fetal brain development and male reproductive tract development [S3]. People who eat packaged and processed food — essentially everyone — would get less phthalate exposure, and the bill specifically directs regulators to account for the higher exposure levels found among Black and Latina women and among workers who handle the materials [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bans all ortho-phthalate chemicals from food contact substances — including tubing used in commercial dairy operations, lid gaskets, food-prep gloves, conveyor belts, and packaging — effective two years after enactment, and voids existing FDA approvals of these uses.
Requires the FDA to review its non-food regulated products for public phthalate exposure and publish a public report within one year, so consumers can see where the chemicals show up.

Directs regulators to consider effects on vulnerable groups — pregnant women, infants, children, the elderly, and exposed workers — and the documented higher exposure among Black and Latina women when evaluating any proposed phthalate substitute.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall on chemical manufacturers that produce ortho-phthalates and on food producers, packagers, and dairies that would need to switch tubing, gaskets, gloves, conveyor belts, and packaging to phthalate-free alternatives within two years. Some of that cost could show up in food prices, though substitutes exist.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food packaging and plastic chemical makers

drawbacks.text: Food producers and packagers would bear the cost of replacing tubing, gaskets, gloves, and packaging within two years, and some of that cost could be passed to consumers in the form of higher food prices.

The ban covers every ortho-phthalate as a class rather than assessing each chemical individually, which supporters would call precautionary and critics would call overbroad, since existing FDA rules had approved certain phthalate uses as safe under specific conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit side is substantial: the bill's own findings cite prenatal exposure harming brain development and male reproductive development, and note that phthalates leach from everyday dairy tubing, gloves, and packaging [S3]. The costs are real but bounded — a two-year transition to substitutes for food-processing equipment, some of which already exist as the bill anticipates by creating a faster petition process for alternatives. The main honest weakness is the blunt class-wide ban rather than chemical-by-chemical safety review. On balance, the bill offers a meaningful public health protection at a moderate, transitionable compliance cost.

outcome.mechanism: It got referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and died there when the Congress ended without anyone scheduling a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 6, 2021, with one cosponsor, Rep. Katie Porter.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee three days later and then to the Health Subcommittee on August 9, 2021.
No further action was recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill never received a markup, a floor vote, or any committee vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Phthalate producers and food packaging and processing companies are better off, since they kept operating under the existing rules that allow these chemicals in food contact materials. No member had to cast a recorded vote on the question.

for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to ban ortho-phthalates as food contact substances

against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill

against.what_they_did: Received the referral after the full committee and took no action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for any vote; both of its sponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led Energy and Commerce Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: Phthalate producers would lose the food-contact market entirely after two years, since the bill deems any use of these chemicals unsafe and voids existing approvals [S3]. Their interest in the current rules runs against the health protections the bill offers eaters.

Food packagers, commercial dairies, and processors would have to replace tubing, gaskets, gloves, and conveyor belts with phthalate-free alternatives within two years [S2, S3]. They would bear the compliance cost, while the public gets lower exposure from packaged and processed food.
